opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the key thing to recognize is that no production system relies on a single safety mechanism. You typically have several layers: the model's own trained behavior, a system prompt with policy instructions, input classifiers that look at what the user is asking, output classifiers that check what the model produces, and sometimes retrieval filters or post-hoc monitoring on top of that. The question isn't "is the model safe?" but "is the whole stack safe, and where does it break?"

Red-team queries are really useful for answering that, but only if you're deliberate about how you use them. If you throw a big set of adversarial prompts at the full system and just report an aggregate attack success rate, you learn very little. You get one number, and you don't know which layer caught what, which layers are redundant, or where the real gaps are.

What I find more productive is to run the same red-team set against each layer in isolation and then in combination. You can ask: what fraction of these attacks does the base model refuse on its own? What does the input classifier catch? What slips past both and only gets stopped at the output filter? That gives you a sort of attribution picture. Sometimes you discover that two layers are catching exactly the same easy cases and both missing the same hard ones, which means you have the appearance of defense in depth without the substance. Ideally your layers have uncorrelated failure modes, and red teaming is how you measure that correlation.

The second thing is that the composition of the red-team set matters enormously. If your queries are mostly blunt, obviously harmful requests, every layer will look great. The interesting signal comes from the long tail: multi-turn escalation, role-play framings, requests split across innocuous-looking pieces, low-resource languages, encoding tricks, and domain-specific cases where you need expertise to even recognize harm. So I'd advocate for building the red-team data with a taxonomy behind it, harm categories crossed with attack strategies, so you can report results per cell and notice that, say, your output classifier is strong in English but weak on code-switched inputs.

Third, you have to look at the other side of the ledger. Every layer you add also has a false positive rate. If you only evaluate on adversarial queries, you'll keep stacking defenses and never notice that you're now refusing legitimate medical or security questions. So pairing red-team sets with borderline-but-benign contrast sets is essential. That tells you whether a layer is actually discriminating or just being more conservative across the board.

Finally, it has to be a loop rather than a one-time audit. The failures you find become training data for the model, examples for classifier retraining, or updates to policy. But once you've patched against a set, it's no longer a fair test, so you need fresh red teaming, ideally including people who weren't involved in building the defenses, plus some held-out sets you never train on, so you can tell real robustness apart from just memorizing last round's attacks.

So in short: red teaming is most valuable when it's treated as a measurement instrument for the system's structure, showing which layer is doing the work, where failures are correlated, and what you're paying in over-refusal, rather than as a single pass/fail score.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes adversarial harm queries from borderline-but-benign contrast sets, including tricky cases that should not trigger refusal.

r002.rationale: It proposes running the same red-team set through layers and measuring what each layer catches and what gets through to later layers.

r003.rationale: It recommends a taxonomy of harm categories and attack strategies, with results reported per category-strategy cell to expose specific weaknesses.

r004.rationale: It recommends fresh red teaming after patches and held-out sets, but does not propose rerunning a fixed set over time to measure improvement.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that red-team queries are really the only way you find out what your defenses actually do, as opposed to what you designed them to do. When you build a layered system, you have maybe an input classifier, you have the model itself with whatever safety training it got, you have an output filter, maybe some retrieval-side guardrails if you're doing RAG. On paper, each of those layers has a job. But in practice you don't know where the failures land until someone actively tries to break it.

So the first thing red-team queries give you is attribution. When a harmful output gets through, you want to know which layer should have caught it and didn't. Did the input classifier miss it because the attack was phrased as a hypothetical or embedded in a long document? Did the model comply when it should have refused? Did the output filter not recognize the content because it was obfuscated or split across turns? If you log every layer's decision for every red-team query, you get a kind of failure map, and that tells you where to invest. Very often what we find is that the layers are correlated in ways you didn't expect. They all fail on the same class of attack because they were all trained or built on similar assumptions about what harmful requests look like.

The second thing is that red-teaming forces you to think in terms of coverage rather than individual test cases. One jailbreak is an anecdote. What you want is a taxonomy, so you can say, we've probed role-play framings, we've probed multi-turn escalation, we've probed encoding tricks, we've probed domain-specific stuff like finance or medical advice, and here's the pass rate per category per layer. That's what lets you have an honest conversation about risk with people who aren't ML researchers.

And then the third piece, which I think gets underappreciated, is that the red-team data becomes training and evaluation data. The queries that got through are exactly what you want to add to your classifier training set or your preference data. But you have to be careful about the loop, because if you only ever fix the things your red team found, you overfit to your red team's creativity. So we try to keep a held-out set of attacks that nobody tunes on, and we rotate people and methods, including automated attackers, so the distribution keeps shifting.

The last point I'd make is that a lot of red-teaming over-indexes on the dramatic failures, the model telling you how to do something dangerous. In an enterprise setting, the more common and often more costly failures are quieter: the system confidently giving wrong financial information, leaking something from a document it shouldn't have surfaced, or being manipulated into taking an action through a tool. Red-team queries are just as useful there, but you have to design them for that, which means working closely with the people who understand the domain and the actual deployment, not just the people who know prompt injection tricks.

r001.rationale: The response lists attack categories such as role-play and encoding tricks, but does not distinguish taxonomy-violating queries from tricky but benign queries.

r002.rationale: It proposes logging each layer’s decisions and reporting pass rates by category and layer, but does not clearly propose tracking counts of genuinely malicious queries that survive each successive layer.

r003.rationale: It categorizes attack types and deployment domains, not unsafe outcomes by risk class to identify specific vulnerabilities.

r004.rationale: It mentions a held-out attack set and rotating red-team methods, but does not propose rerunning a fixed query set over time to assess safety improvement.

astra-6.text:
I think the value of red-team queries is that they let you probe where your assumptions about safety break down. You might have several layers—a model trained to refuse certain requests, an input filter, an output filter—and you want to understand both how each layer behaves and whether the system as a whole actually prevents the harmful outcome.

So if a query gets through, the useful question isn’t just, “Did we fail?” It’s, “Which layer was supposed to catch this, and why didn’t it?” Maybe the input filter missed the intent, or the model recognized the intent but complied anyway. And multiple layers can share the same blind spot, so adding another layer doesn’t necessarily give you independent protection.

Then you can turn those findings into regression tests and use them to guide improvements. But you also need fresh attacks and benign queries that look similar, because you don’t want to simply memorize the attacks or make the system refuse everything. Red-teaming helps you discover failure modes; it doesn’t, by itself, establish that a system is safe.

r001.rationale: It mentions benign queries that resemble attacks, but does not distinguish genuinely taxonomy-violating queries from tricky benign red-team queries.

r002.rationale: It discusses identifying which layer failed, but does not propose tracking counts of malicious queries surviving each successive layer.

r003.rationale: It discusses finding failure modes and blind spots, but does not propose categorizing unsafe outcomes by risk class.

r004.rationale: It proposes regression tests and fresh attacks, but does not specify rerunning a fixed query set over time to assess improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to treat red teaming as a way to understand where the defenses break down. A system might have safeguards in the training, instructions that govern its behavior, and filters around the inputs and outputs. A successful red-team query tells you that something got through that combination, but you still need to understand which layer failed and why.

And even when the system blocks a query, there’s useful information there. Did an early layer catch it, or did every layer except the last one fail? Those are very different situations, even though the user sees the same outcome.

You can then turn those findings into regression tests and test variations of the attack. The goal is to fix the underlying failure mode rather than just block a particular phrase. And you have to evaluate that alongside legitimate requests, because a system that refuses everything would look very safe on an attack benchmark, but it wouldn’t be particularly useful.

r001.rationale: The response mentions evaluating legitimate requests, but it does not distinguish taxonomy-violating queries from tricky but benign red-team queries.

r002.rationale: It discusses identifying which defense layer failed, but does not propose tracking counts of genuinely malicious queries surviving each successive layer.

r003.rationale: It proposes identifying layer failures and underlying failure modes, but not categorizing unsafe outcomes by risk class.

r004.rationale: It suggests creating regression tests and trying attack variations, but does not specify rerunning a fixed query set over time to assess improvement.
